reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A high-grade sarcoma of adults that shows no identifiable line of differentiation despite thorough evaluation, formerly termed malignant fibrous histiocytoma
Essentially a diagnosis of exclusion, made only after immunohistochemistry and, where relevant, molecular testing have ruled out specific sarcoma types
Most often arises in the deep soft tissue of the extremities, particularly the thigh, and in the retroperitoneum, typically in older adults
Usually presents as a rapidly enlarging, deep, painless soft-tissue mass
Genomically complex with highly aberrant karyotypes rather than a defining fusion, reflecting its undifferentiated nature
Diagnosis requires a broad immunohistochemical panel that is negative or non-specific for lineage-defining markers, distinguishing it from dedifferentiated liposarcoma and other pleomorphic sarcomas
Wide surgical excision with adequate margins is the cornerstone, commonly combined with radiotherapy for local control, and chemotherapy is considered in selected high-risk cases
An aggressive tumour with substantial local recurrence and metastatic potential, chiefly to the lungs
reference.pathophysiology: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma is a high-grade malignant mesenchymal tumour defined by the absence of any recognisable line of differentiation after comprehensive pathological assessment. It is genomically complex, marked by extensive chromosomal instability, copy-number aberrations, and frequent alterations in tumour-suppressor pathways such as TP53 and RB1, without the single recurrent translocation that characterises many other sarcomas. This lack of a defining differentiation programme and its accumulated genetic damage account for its pleomorphic morphology and aggressive behaviour. Because several specific sarcomas can appear undifferentiated, the diagnosis is reached only by excluding them through immunohistochemistry and molecular studies.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to define deep extent and relation to neurovascular structures
Whole-body functional imaging for staging in high-grade disease
Core or open biopsy with careful tract planning
Broad immunohistochemical panel to exclude specific lines of differentiation
Molecular testing (including MDM2 for possible dedifferentiated liposarcoma) to exclude defined entities
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging deep soft-tissue mass in an older adult
A large retroperitoneal mass with compressive symptoms
New pain or neurological deficit from local invasion
New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
reference.prognosis: This is an aggressive high-grade sarcoma with significant risk of local recurrence and distant metastasis; prognosis depends on tumour size, depth, grade, site, and completeness of resection, with large, deep, retroperitoneal, or metastatic tumours faring worse.
pitfalls: Labelling a tumour undifferentiated without excluding dedifferentiated liposarcoma by MDM2 testing
Failing to perform a sufficiently broad immunohistochemical workup to exclude specific sarcoma types
Poor biopsy tract planning that compromises subsequent limb-sparing surgery
Underestimating the extent of retroperitoneal disease and achieving inadequate margins
Overlooking pulmonary metastatic surveillance in high-grade disease
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Manage as high grade extremity or truncal soft tissue sarcoma since UPS follows the general sarcoma paradigm rather than a disease specific protocol
Function sparing complete surgical excision with clear margins is the backbone of curative treatment for localized disease
Add radiotherapy for deep, large, high grade tumors or close margins, delivered either before or after surgery since both sequences show similar local control and survival

Consider perioperative chemotherapy with an anthracycline plus an alkylating agent on an individualized basis for large, deep, high grade tumors, particularly histologies felt to be more chemo responsive
Consider re-excision and or adjuvant radiotherapy after an unplanned prior excision given the higher local recurrence risk
Use an anthracycline based regimen as standard first line therapy for unresectable or metastatic disease
Consider combination anthracycline plus alkylating agent therapy in patients with good performance status when a higher response rate is needed, such as before attempting metastasectomy
Consider a gemcitabine plus taxane combination as a reasonable first line alternative to single agent anthracycline
For second line therapy after anthracycline failure, consider a gemcitabine taxane combination, single agent ifosfamide, pazopanib, or dacarbazine
Consider clinical trial enrollment at any point given the limited number of active agents, especially after first line therapy fails
Consider surgical resection of limited, resectable pulmonary or other metastases in selected patients
Use radiotherapy for palliation of symptomatic metastatic sites and tailor treatment intensity to symptoms and patient preference rather than escalating reflexively

Perform surveillance with periodic clinical exam of the primary site and chest imaging given the lung is the dominant site of distant spread, using a risk adapted interval as a general oncology standard

Refer any suspected case to a specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary center before biopsy or excision given the diagnosis of exclusion workup and the risk that poor biopsy planning compromises limb sparing surgery
